exam: A 58‑year‑old man presents with sudden left arm weakness lasting 30 min that resolved. What is the next immediate step? — Calculate ABCD2 score, arrange urgent brain imaging and start aspirin.
How does the ABCD2 score influence management? — Higher scores (>4) trigger admission, urgent carotid imaging, and possible dual antiplatelet therapy.

A patient with known HIV on protease inhibitors presents with TIA. Which risk factor needs special attention? — Dyslipidaemia from protease inhibitors; ensure statin therapy and monitor liver function.
Why is aspirin preferred over clopidogrel as first‑line in most TIA patients? — Aspirin is widely available, cheap, and has a well‑established safety profile in low‑resource settings.
What feature distinguishes a TIA from a Todd’s paresis after a seizure? — Todd’s paresis follows a witnessed seizure and often has post‑ictal confusion; TIA lacks seizure activity.
A patient cannot afford carotid Doppler. How can you still assess for carotid disease? — Perform careful auscultation for carotid bruits and refer for surgical assessment if high clinical suspicion.
When is anticoagulation contraindicated in TIA? — Active bleeding, severe uncontrolled hypertension, or recent intracranial haemorrhage.

What lifestyle advice reduces recurrent TIA risk in a rural Tanzanian community? — Stop smoking, reduce salt intake, control hypertension, adhere to antithrombotic therapy, and treat malaria promptly.
ai.title: Transient Ischaemic Attack
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A brief, reversible neurological deficit caused by temporary cerebral ischemia. Diagnosis relies on symptom timing, exclusion of stroke mimics, and urgent risk stratification. Management focuses on rapid secondary prevention, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: No new infarct on CT/MRI (if available)
sections.p: A transient ischaemic attack is a focal neurological deficit lasting <24 h, usually <1 h, without evidence of acute infarction on imaging.

sections.p: Risk of early stroke is stratified with the ABCD2 score; higher scores demand urgent investigation and treatment.
Most TIAs are embolic or atherothrombotic; in low‑resource East African settings, add infectious and hematologic contributors.
